📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

Sources indicate that but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

Industry observers note that the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

It has been revealed that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

Sources indicate that at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

It has been revealed that tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

In a recent development, to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

Recent findings suggest that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

Recent findings suggest that this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It revealed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

It has been revealed that what makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

It has been revealed that to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Recent findings suggest that their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become key simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

Industry observers note that the team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

In a recent development, raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

Industry observers note that in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a fresh aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists upcoming ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

According to recent reports, the implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

It has been revealed that that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a upcoming foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

According to recent reports, for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • 25 percent of those who participated voted to recognise the union, while 75 percent voted against.
  • According to recent reports, jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar Games told Eurogamer: "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games employees have voted against official recognition of the Rockstar Game Workers Union, with 93.2 percent of staff participating in the vote.

25 percent of those who participated voted to recognise the union, while 75 percent voted against. If it had been approved, it would have been the largest recognised union in the UK video game industry by a large margin. While the union will still exist and organise, Rockstar Games will not have to recognise the union as a representing body for staff at the studio, and is not obligated to attend regular meetings with the body.

According to recent reports, jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar Games told Eurogamer: "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together.".

Sources indicate that the Rockstar Union also released a statement following the outcome of this vote, saying Rockstar employees will continue to organise despite the lack of recognition. It reads:.

In a recent development, "For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn't a sign to retreat, it's a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen.

"Whilst we haven't emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for upcoming kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.

According to recent reports, "A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it's one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We'll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against Al and layoffs.

"The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands.".

In a recent development, rockstar employees represented by the union are still awaiting the verdict from the Rockstar Games vs IWGB employment tribunal legal case, of which the final verdict is still pending. This case was kicked off by the sudden firing of employees present in a union Discord server. The employees claim this was an attempt at union busting by Rockstar, while the tech giant denies this, saying it was for breaking confidentiality agreements.

  • Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion.

Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape.

This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. The explosive remnants mixing with gas in the interstellar medium created this glowing, blue cloud.

Industry observers note that this celestial scene was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), that was created by the U.S. Department of Energy. The camera is installed on the National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

This image of a colossal, cosmic "fish" was captured by a camera meant to study the illusive effects of dark energy, which is the name scientists have given for whatever mysterious something is causing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate.

The camera is used as part of the Dark Energy Survey, a six-year, international collaboration in which scientists have collected observations of hundreds of millions of galaxies, thousands of supernova and additional details about our cosmos that could help to fill in the picture of the nature of dark energy.

And while researchers this past January revealed the initial result of this six-year survey, scientists continue to explore the possibilities of dark energy with DECam alongside instruments like the recently-introduced Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

However, while the survey has lofty goals with its DECam data, the camera can also capture beautiful imagery like this cerulean wisp thousands of light-years away.

Industry observers note that chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rob NelsonRockstar Games.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto 6Â contains a surprising but cool cameo hidden near the very end of the game’s main story. So when I got a chance to chat with Rockstar’s head of production, Rob Nelson, about GTA 6 ahead of the game’s launch, I had to ask about this moment, how it came about, and what it means for the character.

But uh… major spoilers. Seriously, if you’re a big GTA nerd and love to be surprised, turn around right now and stop reading. You’ll thank me later when you reach this point and get to experience it unspoiled. For those who don’t care or who can’t resist the siren’s call of secrets being revealed, keep scrolling past the warning. Just don’t yell at me later!

Industry observers note that as you approach the final missions in the game, Jason and Lucia start working with Giorgio, a very rich shipping magnate who works with Eastern European criminals to smuggle drugs across the ocean on his big ships. And things aren’t going well, forcing Giorgio to work with Jason, Lucia, and others on a big, ambitious initiative to steal back all the cocaine confiscated by the Coast Guard as part of a large heist. But before they can pull off the heist, a higher-up from the big Balkan cartel Giorgio has been working with arrives to kill him for screwing up, but gives him one more chance to get back the coke. That badass hitman? Niko Bellic, the playable protagonist of 2008’s Grand Theft Auto IV.

Here’s the scene from GTA 6 in which he appears:.

Recent findings suggest that I asked Nelson if they’d planned to include Niko from the start, and he tells me that they hadn’t. Instead, he told me that the cameo came about “very organically.”.

“[Early in development], we had Giorgio and we had him working with a sort of Balkan cartel,” explained Nelson. The GTA 6 boss further explained that this whole storyline was based on research they’d done about actual Italian shipping companies that allegedly smuggled drugs for various gangs in South America. Apparently, a boat run by such a organization was carrying 20 tons of coke when it was raided by U.S. officials. That number should sound familiar to anyone who has played the later missions of GTA 6, as that’s the amount of coke seized by the Coast Guard in the game.Â.

“Giorgio is not really a criminal. He’s a sort of wealthy shipping magnate who’s in league with these criminals,” mentioned Nelson.

“But it was sort of that same [real-world] idea. And then we needed someone from the Balkan cartel to show up. It just grew very organically, and it’s like, well, who would he be working with from the Balkan end of the organization? When Giorgio fucks up, who’s going to come down to deal with him? And I got an idea.”.

In a recent development, nelson says Niko’s story was sort of “left open” after the events of GTA IV.Â “He’s still kicking around. He’s still in play,” he told Kotaku. Nelson also confirmed original voice actor Michael Holick returned for the role. When I asked if it was nice to have him back and work with him again, Nelson responded with a smile: “Very much, yeah.”Â.

In a recent development, I asked Nelson if this cameo confirms anything about which ending is canon in GTA IV, and Nelson wouldn’t say one way or the other and pointed out that nothing Niko says or does in either cutscene indicates a specific canon ending for that game. He did confirm that Niko will be going back to Liberty City after all this and that it’s been his home since GTA IV.Â.

There’s one more great detail included in this cameo moment. After the cutscene ends, players hear the mission-complete jingle from GTA IV play instead of one of GTA 6‘s various mission-complete jingles. According to Nelson, that was a “late addition.”.

According to recent reports, “For a long time it was like a normal [GTA 6] stinger, and we played it and…” Nelson made an meh face. “I got on with Yvonne and noted, ‘Can we put the [mimics the GTA IV mission complete jingle] in there?'” And they did, which was a wonderful touch to an already amazing moment.Â.

When we talked about Niko Bellic in GTA 6, Nelson did admit that he hoped “it stays secret for a bit.” Sadly, a lot of people rushed through GTA 6 and posted videos of Niko last week, less than three days after the game’s launch. Welp.

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 has broken another livestreaming record. After attracting more viewers across livestreaming platforms than any game ever on its launch day, Rockstar's open-world crime sim has reportedly continued to dominate on platforms like Twitch, YouTube, and Kick.

Recent findings suggest that over its first seven days on sale, GTA 6 has amassed over 420m hours watched, according to Streams Charts. That's nearly three times more than the previous record, held by Valorant's closed beta in April 2020. In fact, that 420m hours tally is more than the first-week watch time achieved by Valorant, Elden Ring, Diablo 4, and Lost Ark combined.

Sources indicate that as for the livestreaming platforms that saw the largest audiences for GTA 6, YouTube reportedly had the lead in average audience numbers during the first six hours of launch, but Twitch took over in content volume in the days that followed. #195. Industry News: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1134 w)

Industry News: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

Recent findings suggest that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an key role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

It has been revealed that chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are at the moment beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Sources indicate that in the upcoming system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

In a recent development, many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

Recent findings suggest that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Sources indicate that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

In a recent development, the research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Industry observers note that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

Recent findings suggest that "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments demonstrated that the latest architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

According to recent reports, however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising upcoming route toward making those machines a reality.

#194. Exploring the Indium phosphide supply chain — the material constraint tightening the optical interconnect bottleneck

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2524 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Exploring the Indium phosphide supply chain — the material constraint tightening the optical interconnect bottleneck

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Tomshardware)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that indium phosphide (InP) is a compound material used in specialized chip-making.
  • In a recent development, inP chips have powered high-speed lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and various other optical components used across the telecommunications industry and defense for decades.
  • As AI clusters hit the physical limits of moving enormous amounts of data over copper, the industry began the switch to optical interconnects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that indium phosphide (InP) is a compound material used in specialized chip-making. Unlike silicon, which is the fundamental building block for mainstream logic and memory chips, InP — made from indium and phosphorus — is mainly used to manufacture highly specialized photonic and high-frequency electronic chips, largely due to its outstanding optical properties. Its immensely expensive and complex manufacturing process also makes it impractical for the large volumes and die sizes needed for logic and memory chips. With the industry predicting a shortfall of this crucial material right as the shift to optical interconnects in data centers begins, we explore the current state of the supply chain.

In a recent development, inP chips have powered high-speed lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and various other optical components used across the telecommunications industry and defense for decades. While the InP supply chain was relatively small and highly specialized, it was generally stable and sufficient to meet global demands.

Then came the AI boom. As AI clusters hit the physical limits of moving enormous amounts of data over copper, the industry began the switch to optical interconnects. First came ever-faster optical transceivers. Now the industry is transitioning to silicon photonics, near-packaged optics, and co-packaged optics, bringing optical links progressively closer to the processors themselves. InP is central to much of this transition, building the critical active optical components needed to turn electrical data into light and back again.

Individual AI data centers are already being built around hundreds of thousands of accelerators, with upcoming gigawatt-scale buildouts expected to house millions. Connecting those processors translates into demand for millions upon millions of indispensable optical components, all relying on the same relatively tiny InP supply chain.

It has been revealed that japan's Sumitomo Electric and U.S.-headquartered AXT together account for almost 80% of global InP substrate manufacturing, with JX Advanced Metals adding roughly another 10%. AXT, however, manufactures most of its InP substrates in China, where exports now require government licenses, further exacerbating the situation. It gets worse: China accounts for around 70% of global refined indium output, which is recovered as a byproduct of processing zinc. Export controls mean that restrictions apply to both the material itself and the finished wafer.

The resulting squeeze is already sending ripples across the industry, with several companies predicting shortfalls. Michael Hurlston, CEO of optical-component manufacturer Lumentum, said in July that the firm's InP fabs were shipping more than 30% below customer demand, despite rapid capacity expansion. Coherent also described InP capacity as the “primary constraint” on its transceiver business.

According to recent reports, A simple solution would be to expand the supply chain. However, growing large, low-defect InP crystals is difficult, while qualifying latest suppliers requires time that doesn't align with the industry's demand. Furthermore, expanding substrate and laser-fabrication capacity can take years. Meanwhile, to secure optical components capacity for its accelerators, Nvidia has invested $2 billion each in Lumentum and Coherent, attaching multibillion-dollar purchase commitments and future capacity rights to both deals. Both companies, along with several others in the supply chain, are frantically pursuing solutions.

Recent findings suggest that indium phosphide belongs to the III-V family of compound semiconductors, named after the periodic-table groups of their constituent elements; in InP’s case, indium and phosphorus. Its better-known relatives include gallium arsenide and gallium nitride.

According to recent reports, indium phosphide’s distinguishing property, which separates it from silicon, is its direct bandgap, measured at about 1.34 eV at room temperature. In a direct-bandgap material, electrons dropping across the gap release their energy efficiently as photons, making the material particularly useful for lasers and other active optical devices.

It has been revealed that silicon, on the other hand, has an indirect bandgap, meaning that the same transition requires an additional interaction with a crystal lattice and mostly sheds its energy as heat instead. Therefore, while the material can — in silicon photonics — guide, split, and modulate light using structures fabricated with mature CMOS processes, it does not produce the light beam. As a result, Modern silicon-photonics systems commonly rely on a III-V laser source, most commonly based on the InP material system, to provide the light that the silicon circuitry manipulates.

The fiber-optic wavelength window’s alignment with InP's properties is another reason for the material's ubiquity. Modern telecom and data-center links commonly operate around 1,310 nm and 1,550 nm, where optical fiber exhibits favorable transmission characteristics. Pure InP itself does not emit at those exact wavelengths. However, InGaAsP and InAlGaAs alloys, which are grown on lattice-matched InP substrates, can have their bandgaps engineered for those bands. InGaAs layers on InP are also highly effective photodetectors at telecom wavelengths.

Recent findings suggest that these characteristics and functionalities make the InP platform critical to many active functions in optical communications, including distributed-feedback (DFB) lasers, electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs), continuous-wave (CW) lasers, semiconductor optical amplifiers, photodetectors, and complete photonic integrated circuits. Silicon photonics and InP consequently complement each other. Silicon provides scalable optical circuitry, while InP provides efficient light generation and several high-performance active optical devices.

According to recent reports, beyond photonics, InP is also commonly used in high-frequency electronic chips. Electrons move through the material far faster than through silicon, giving it strong high-frequency performance that makes it suitable for millimeter-wave and terahertz electronics, radar receivers, and high-speed data converters. This market is much smaller than photonics, but it has few substitutes at the top of the frequency range.

Industry observers note that inP lasers and transceivers have been converting electrical signals into light for long-haul fiber networks, metro links, submarine cables, and eventually shorter-reach data-center connections for decades. Despite 5G rollouts driving demand higher, the indium phosphide supply chain remained a stable, moderately sized business with predictable growth. The AI boom has now driven demand up by several orders of magnitude.

Modern AI clusters can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnected accelerators that continuously exchange data. Copper remains a cheap, effective connector over short distances, but electrical losses, signal integrity, and power requirements progressively worsen as bandwidth and distance increase. This has led to the rapid adoption of optical interconnects.

In this setup, a modulator encodes electrical data from the switch or accelerator onto light from a laser. Fiber cables then carry it across the link to a photodetector that converts the received photons back into an electrical signal. In pluggable transceivers, many of these functions are integrated into a compact module plugged into the front of a network switch, with InP-based components executing several steps in the process.

According to recent reports, lumentum's 200G EML, for example, monolithically combines a wavelength-locked DFB laser and an electro-absorption modulator on its InP platform, and is designed for 200-Gbps-per-lane links used in 1.6T transceivers. Coherent is producing InP EMLs, high-power CW lasers, and high-speed photodiodes for the same generation of hardware. As aggregate link speeds move from 400G and 800G to 1.6T and beyond, the number and performance of these InP-based optical components become increasingly notable.

At the same time, the industry is bringing optics right to the board with co-packaged optics (CPO) to further shorten the distance data travels. Conventional pluggable optics leave around 15 to 30 centimeters (5.90 to 11.81 inches) of high-speed copper trace between the switch ASIC and the optical module. CPO brings the optical engine onto the accelerator package as a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip, shrinking that electrical path and reducing power consumption. Nvidia's Quantum-X and Spectrum-X photonics switches are among the first major AI platforms built around that approach.

Recent findings suggest that while they integrate several optical functions onto the boards, PIC chips do not generate the laser. CPO and silicon-photonics designs still mostly use external InP CW lasers to supply light to the silicon photonic circuits, further consolidating the demand for indium phosphide in AI data centers and the industry as a whole.

As a result of the enormous, rapidly expanding market for the material, indium phosphide’s supply chain is constrained at several points, starting with the raw material itself. Unlike many metals which are mined from dedicated deposits, indium is typically recovered as a trace byproduct of processing zinc sulfide ore. Manufacturers then combine high-purity indium and phosphorus and grow them into a single-crystal InP ingot, or boule, which they process into substrate wafers with tightly controlled properties. Next, manufacturers grow extremely thin epitaxial layers of InP-related compounds over it, commonly using metal-organic chemical vapor deposition. The epiwafer then goes through several chip-making processes and module assembly to become optical chips and devices.

Recent findings suggest that indium production's dependence on Zinc processing creates bottlenecks in InP's supply chain, right at the beginning of the stream. The USGS put global primary refined indium production at roughly 1,100 tonnes in 2025, with China accounting for 760 tonnes. For context, the BBC estimates that 30,000 tonnes of electronic-grade silicon used exclusively to make microchips are mined yearly. The United States imports all of the InP it consumes, producing nothing. Meanwhile, indium substrate manufacturers Japan's Sumitomo and JX Metals source more than 90% of their high-purity indium feedstock from China, meaning even non-Chinese substrate makers begin their process with Chinese material.

According to recent reports, further downstream, at the substrate manufacturing level, Sumitomo Electric holds roughly 40% of the global InP substrate market, U.S.-based AXT around 35%, and JX Advanced Metals about 10%. Together, the three control more than 90% of capacity. Although AXT is headquartered in California, most of its InP substrate production runs through its Beijing Tongmei subsidiary, which puts it directly under China's export licensing regime. Other fringe substrate manufacturers include Freiberger Compound Materials in Germany and a growing set of Chinese entrants, including Yunnan Germanium.

The supply chain is also highly concentrated at the device and component level, with Coherent and Lumentum dominating Western laser and component production. IQE supplies epitaxial wafers, and Japanese firms, including Mitsubishi Electric, supply laser components. Chinese module makers such as Innolight and Eoptolink assemble a large share of the world's finished 800G modules, pairing Western lasers with Broadcom and Marvell DSPs. We recently explored how this entanglement complicates any attempt to decouple the two ecosystems, even as the FCC is considering a ban on Chinese optical hardware. Coherent primarily sources substrates from AXT, while Lumentum relies heavily on Sumitomo and JX.

In a recent development, on the technical side, wafer-size limitations in InP semiconductors add another constraint. While silicon logic and memory moved to 300-mm wafers in the early 2000s, the InP industry is only now transitioning from 3-inch to 6-inch (150-mm) production; primarily because the material is brittle, expensive, and grown in small boules, factors that limit wafer size. Doubling the wafer diameter gives four times the area. Coherent's six-inch line, for example, yields more than four times as many devices as its three-inch line at a lower cost per die. On the other hand, moving a fab to six-inch requires latest crystal-growth recipes, new handling equipment, new process qualification, and extensive customer requalification.

Recent findings suggest that the supply chain was already struggling under these constraints when, in February 2025, Beijing placed InP, trimethylindium, triethylindium, and the technology used to produce them under export controls, requiring licenses for overseas shipments. AXT called the export controls its most significant current challenge, noting that even with sufficient capacity and strong demand, its ability to ship outside China depends on Chinese licensing decisions.

The widening gap between demand and InP industry output points to a fast-approaching shortfall. Coherent first warned of an InP shortage on its May earnings call. At the close of its fiscal year in August, CEO Jim Anderson described indium phosphide availability as the company's primary constraint, confirming that transceiver assembly and test capacity were available.

Industry observers note that lumentum CEO Hurlston mentioned in July that telecom customers historically ordered lasers in the hundreds, while Nvidia and the hyperscalers were asking for hundreds of millions. Despite operating multiple InP fabs, Lumentum was shipping more than 30% below customer requirements. Earlier in the year, Hurlston said the tech giant's capacity was sold out through 2027 and probably into 2028, even with the expanded output. In both cases, capacity was mostly bought out via Nvidia’s $4 billion investment.

In a recent development, to ease the multifaceted bottleneck, the industry is pursuing several solutions simultaneously, primarily expansions. Coherent is expanding its Sherman, Texas campus, reportedly described as the first and largest high-volume 6-inch InP semiconductor manufacturing facility. Washington signed a letter of intent in June for up to $50 million in CHIPS Act funding for the expansion. Coherent is now on track to double internal InP output in 2026, one quarter ahead of its original blueprint, and more than double it again by the end of 2027, while also adding 6-inch production in Sweden and Zurich.

Lumentum, meanwhile, is converting a 240,000-square-foot former Qorvo gallium-arsenide facility in North Carolina, which it bought for about $18 million, into another InP fab. The relevance of these expansions largely depends on the downstream InP substrate supply. Lumentum signed an agreement in July to reserve AXT InP substrate capacity through 2031, with an initial $43.5 million deposit and another $43.5 million payment contemplated for 2028. Coherent signed its own three-year 6-inch supply agreement with AXT a month earlier and prepaid $22.3 million against committed capacity.

The substrate suppliers are also expanding in kind. AXT is channeling fresh funds into Beijing Tongmei to double capacity by the end of 2026 and double it again in 2027. Similarly, JX Advanced Metals plans to invest roughly ¥120 billion ($746 million) through FY2030 to lift capacity seven to ten times above FY2025 levels, its largest-ever commitment in semiconductor materials.

Indium production — the uppermost stage of the stream — is far less active, with the biggest hurdle being the reliance on Zinc production. Global zinc mine production hasn't grown materially since 2011, sitting at or below 13 million tonnes a year, according to analysts. Wood Mackenzie expects just 0.1% growth in 2026. On the other hand, not everyone expects the crunch to last. LightCounting estimated in April that optical component demand exceeded supply by about 30% but projected that shortages would largely clear by the end of 2026 as new capacity comes online.

Sources indicate that there are also viable, albeit slow, technical workarounds to ease the crunch. Heterogeneous integration bonds InP onto silicon to combine the strengths of both, while quantum dot lasers offer better temperature stability for uncooled operation. Furthermore, researchers continue to push InP quantum dot structures grown directly on silicon substrates. While these do not remove indium from the equation, they change how much each device needs and how it attaches, reducing consumption. Photonics is widely viewed as one of AI's major bottlenecks. However, the indium phosphide supply chain is itself tightening that bottleneck.

Sources indicate that etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in substantial tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

The fresh feature, however, lets you set an independent volume for all alarms and timers, not just those in the Sleep Schedule.

Alarms, Timers, Alerts, and System Sounds are set to match your ringtone volume by default, but you can turn them off in the Sounds and Haptics setting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A football referee has denied accusations of being drunk after being removed from a match at halftime following a bizarre incident in which he highlighted a yellow card to a goalkeeper nearly half the pitch away from a foul.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was officiating an AFC Champions League Two match between the United Arab Emirates’ Al Jazira and Iran’s Gol Gohar when his decision-making raised eyebrows.

In the 32nd minute, Hattab awarded a free kick following a foul by Al Jazira’s Felicio Milson and approached the winger with a yellow card in hand.

However, as reported by the Daily Mail, the referee appeared to receive a message through his earpiece before suddenly changing direction and walking toward Al Jazira goalkeeper Ersin Destanoglu.

Despite being nowhere near the foul, the stunned goalkeeper was shown a yellow card.

Hattab eventually overturned the decision after consulting his fourth official, while Milson avoided receiving what would have been his second yellow card of the match.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among the many, many side activities you can do in GTA 6, there's powerwashing. Relatively early on, as part of Chapter 1's Down to Earth mission, Jason whips out his nozzle and blasts Brian's boat to a gleaming sheen. Disappointingly for powerwashing fans, though, it's a bit of a one-and-done gag, never to return. But powerwashing is powerwashing, and we immediately wondered what the experts made of it all. Had Rockstar, with its legendary attention to detail, accurately captured the intricacies of powerwashing in those leisurely moments of carefree squirting?

According to recent reports, A question had been asked and an answer was required. So who better to cast judgement on the authenticity of Jason's sway-and-spraying than FuturLab, the studio behind the delightfully zen PowerWash Simulator series? Thus, in a moment of whimsy, I asked if it might like to 'review' GTA 6's hosiest activity. At best, I was hoping for a cheeky little statement; I certainly wasn't expecting a major chunk of the PowerWash Simulator 2 team to join in the fun. "Fair to say," the intermediary PR noted, "the Futurlab team was excited about this one!".

So what's the verdict? Let us turn to the pros. "They've got the sounds and satisfaction of clearly a nice shiny flat surface just right," PowerWash Simulator 2 lead game designer Nick McCarthy opined, "but where's the ding!? 0/10, needs 200 percent more layers of muck and 20 percent more parkour." And promptly a trend emerged. "Great visuals, satisfying feel, but lacks the crucial ding and went by too quickly to listen to a podcast," senior programmer Will Dyball wrote. Then still more sadness for the lack of PowerWash Simulator's most motivating sound: "Didn't hear a ding," associate publishing producer Jess Crosby wrote. "Must have missed a bit.".

Industry observers note that A few team members also spotted some powerwashing faux pas. "No soap?" wrote 3D artist Eilidh Norris. "Rookie mistake, Jason." Programmer Jordan Lewis also reckoned Jason was making things unnecessarily hard for himself: "[He'd] have had an easier time had he taken the time to upgrade his washer and purchased some more nozzles," they wrote. "PS. Soap would have gotten that off in a flash." Others had safety concerns: "I find Jason's lack of protective overalls disturbing," mentioned 3D artist Rory Peace, and data principal Russell Young agreed. "Clean speedboat, ruined clothes. Don't want to bring them 'Down to Earth', but we need to talk about PPE." People advisor Sarah Robshaw, meanwhile, spotted a more heinous omission: "Where's the cats????".

Elsewhere, game designer Sam Jenkins was delighted by the powerwashing representation. "I'm so glad that the Art of Powerwashing is being taken more seriously in mainstream games!" they wrote. "However, I think the dirt on the boat is too scarce for that satisfying cleaning contrast to come through.".

According to recent reports, jenkins even had some expert suggestions to make Jason's little squirt-out more rewarding: "Maybe the boat should have been left in a flooded warehouse for 30 years to coat it in grime?" they continued. "Or even have a crushed fruit festival come through town to get some nice substantial colourful blobs all over the boat. Ooh! And we could even have the boat be the home of various squids to get some difficult-to-clean Ink streaked down it too!" Truly the words of someone who takes their powerwashing seriously!

In a recent development, junior build engineer Owen Layton, programmer Jordan Lewis, and lead designer Nick McCarthy also provided 'reviews' in pictoral form, but technical complications mean they'll just have to exist in your imagination. Senior narrative designer Mark Ginbey, though, expressed admiration for all the in-world encouragement players are given. "Some excellent motivational text updates from Cal, like 'Mmhmm, half way there...' to indicate 50 percent completion," they wrote. "But Jason needs to concentrate on the work in hand. A quality powerwasher never talks on the job.".

According to recent reports, senior game designer António Salreta had praise for GTA 6, with one exception: "It's an amazing game with so many fun systems - but. Needs. More. Nozzles." And how's this for a ringing endorsement from senior QA tester Paul Comse? "I love coming home after a hard day of work powerwashing in PowerWash Sim and unwinding by powerwashing some more in GTA," they wrote. But if we're scoring Jason's efforts? "7.8/10, too much water.".

Recent findings suggest that so there you go! The experts have spoken, and I'd call it a success for Rockstar's inaugural attempt at powerwashing, despite a handful of 'must try harders'. An unexpectedly generous response indeed! And if you're curious how FuturLab does it, look no further than last year's PowerWash Simulator 2. And for help with powerwashing in GTA 6, we've got a guide.

8 Essential Thriller Books Everyone Should Read at Least Once

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The safest way to chase an adrenaline rush is to read a captivating thriller book.
  • Take genre staples like Gone Girl or The Silent Patient.
  • Sources indicate that the Oscar-winning Conclave was a surprising front-runner in a year dominated by flashier films like Anora and The Brutalist, and its source material is just as disarmingly good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The safest way to chase an adrenaline rush is to read a captivating thriller book. These stories rely on one or more mysteries to ramp up tension, provoke intellectual curiosity, and deliver a sense of catharsis. Fiction is often a safe space to explore uncomfortable emotions, and thrillers deliver on this front by allowing readers to escape into worlds brimming with danger.

Take genre staples like Gone Girl or The Silent Patient. While the two couldn’t be more different in tone and subject matter, both thrillers heavily rely on misdirection and the recontextualization of events to deliver twists. These picks are a staple in every “must-read” list for good reason, just like the ones Polygon has highlighted below as genre essentials. Without further ado, here are eight thriller books you should read at least once in your life.

Sources indicate that the Oscar-winning Conclave was a surprising front-runner in a year dominated by flashier films like Anora and The Brutalist, and its source material is just as disarmingly good. The premise of a papal conclave held right after the pope’s death might feel a bit too somber, but Conclave unfolds like a tense political thriller that balances breakneck pacing with intricate detail. Jacopo Lomeli is tasked with the responsibility of overseeing the papal conclave in the event of the tragedy, and four cardinals are promptly chosen as leading candidates. But there’s more to the conspiracy than one would expect, turning the novel into a thrilling clash of ideologies that is also a deft exploration of inner conflict.

The Talented Mr. Ripley introduces us to Tom Ripley, famously played by Matt Damon in Anthony Minghella’s 1999 film adaptation and Andrew Scott in Netflix’s Ripley. Tom is struggling to make ends meet in Newly introduced York, prompting him to carry out petty cons. When shipping magnate Herbert Greenleaf approaches Ripley to persuade his son, Dickie, to join the family business, the opportunistic young man readily agrees. Patricia Highsmith presents an unforgettable anti-hero, whose actions follow irrefutable internal logic despite being morally wrong. The novel is a fascinating character study about sociable forms of evil and how they manifest when you least expect it.

A “whodunnit” framework propels most mystery thrillers, but The Secret History operates with a tense, slow-burn “why-done-it” narrative. The novel’s unreliable narrator, Richard Papen, immediately tells us about a murder, a crime for which he is “partly responsible.” This curiosity to understand the why and how makes this dark academia campus novel especially riveting. The novel’s secluded setting in Vermont adds to the isolation of the six tight-knit students at its center, whose obsession with all things Ancient Greece comes with a heavy price. Tartt’s characters are flawed, obnoxious, and compelling, successfully retaining our avid interest despite being deliberately disengaged from the world at large.

It has been revealed that blake Crouch has written engaging sci-fi books like Recursion and Upgrade, and Dark Matter leans heavily into sci-fi thriller territory with its propulsive pacing. The story follows physicist Jason Dessen, who is kidnapped and sent to a parallel universe, where his life plays out differently due to a drastically different choice he made in this timeline. In fact, this version of Jason has built a cube that enables travel between countless alternate worlds, which changes his understanding of quantum mechanics. Dark Matter is easily accessible for anyone, as its convoluted premise unfolds in a way that’s fun and easily digestible. This is undoubtedly popcorn entertainment, meant to be read while you’re waiting at the airport.

In a recent development, david Cronenberg’s adaptation of The Dead Zone is both a taut thriller and a quietly melancholic movie about a man with a strange gift. A child named Johnny Smith problems a prophetic warning after an ice-skating accident, and grows up to become a small-town high school teacher. Things take a turn after an accident-induced coma makes Johnny gain frighteningly accurate psychic abilities, along with a vision of the end of the world. Stephen King’s source material excels in conveying the eerie, lived-in horror of weighing extreme choices to determine the fate of those around us. Johnny’s predicament, although fantastical, feels deeply human in the way the personal and the political seamlessly blend together.

A bona fide bestseller that has been adapted countless times on the screen, Rebecca is the definition of a Gothic novel with exceptional thriller elements. The book opens with an unnamed narrator lamenting that she cannot return to her husband’s estate, as it has been destroyed. Looking back, she recounts how she married the older, wealthy Maximilian de Winter, whose first wife, Rebecca, drowned in a sailing accident. Although the narrator does her best to acclimatize to her latest life, every person at the estate seems haunted by Rebecca’s memory, to the point of undermining the new bride’s sense of self. Rebecca is a timeless classic about memory and identity, one that is also an exemplary entry in 20th-century Gothic fiction.

Stieg Larsson’s “Millennium Trilogy” is spectacular as a whole, but The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo stands out for several reasons. The book introduces us to journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is facing jail time after losing a libel case. Although Blomkvist retreats from the public eye, he takes an interest in a curious disappearance case after meeting Henrik Vanger, the CEO of Vanger Enterprises. Blomkvist, however, isn’t the only person involved, as the exceptionally gifted investigator Lisbeth Salander has been hired to evaluate his history and skill set. The novel is a labyrinth of clues, red herrings, and twists, along with a gritty exploration of abuse and institutional failure.

Recent findings suggest that if you like the Oscar-winning neo-noir mystery, Mystic River, chances are that you’ll also like the book it is based on. Three boys — Dave, Sean, and Jimmy — grow up together in Boston. Tragedy strikes when Dave is abducted, and he returns after managing to escape, deeply traumatized. Fast-forward 25 years; the three men have been shaped by their respective circumstances, brought together by a grisly murder and the unsavory realization that one of them might be involved. Mystic River is a book that delves beneath the surface, compelling us to understand how grief carries on into adulthood. There’s immense thematic weight to this book about the tussle between choice and fatalism in the face of injustice.

#186. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

In a recent development, "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

Industry observers note that for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Recent findings suggest that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

Recent findings suggest that the latest findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

Sources indicate that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The newly introduced approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another notable discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

Recent findings suggest that "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler mentioned. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

Sources indicate that A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

Recent findings suggest that the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring people to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

In a recent development, "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

According to recent reports, the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

Industry observers note that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the memory shortage has gotten so bad that many companies, especially smaller ones, have started establishing “procurement war rooms,” where employees are desperately trying to find memory chip supplies on sites like eBay and trying to figure out how they could make manufacturers offer them even just a small amount of DRAM. This massive shortage has pushed up costs for electronic manufacturers, with some companies forced to increase prices to make up the difference while others cut the specifications of their products while introducing a smaller price bump.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Taiwanese memory module and storage maker Apacer had to take out loans just to have money on hand in case it finds a supply of memory chips. “If chips show up, we take it,” Apacer President Gibson Chen told the publication. “This is crazy, but there is no other way.” Even one of the world’s richest people, Elon Musk, was reportedly having trouble finding memory chips. A portfolio manager claimed that Musk offered Samsung an LTA and even a financial guarantee for new Samsung chip factories, but the manufacturer’s executive chairman, Lee Jae-yong, allegedly answered that everyone else was offering those things already. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also recently went to South Korea to meet with Samsung leadership just to secure more RAM for data centers.

According to recent reports, even though PC builders and enthusiasts were the hardest hit by the 500% climb in memory prices, many other electronics manufacturers are also now feeling the squeeze. Significant companies like Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft could use their scale and resources to pay more and secure massive amounts of memory chip supplies under long-term agreements (LTAs). However, smaller firms would usually have to rely on brokers and whatever’s available to find what they need. Some have reportedly contacted hundreds of brokers and go through online listings, where they would snap up even small batches of just five or 12 units just to have some supply. Others proceed to the gray market, although they must be careful as some unscrupulous sellers mix in batches of used memory chips with brand new orders to inflate their deliveries.

Sources indicate that the scramble for AI compute has caused a massive memory chip shortage, especially as the major three memory chip manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — have focused their production on more lucrative HBM. Both memory chip manufacturers and RAM kit makers are warning of continued shortages, too, with SK hynix saying 2027 will be the “worst year” for memory shortages, while TeamGroup’s CEO noted that it could reach a point where “even money can’t buy goods.” Although the big three manufacturers are building upcoming factories, they’re not expected to go online and start pushing out memory chips until 2028.

It’s difficult for a newly introduced player to enter the memory chip market. Aside from the enormous costs involved in setting up a factory and supply chain to build memory chips, any potential entrant must also license a ton of patents and develop its own technologies before it can start making competitive chips. Even if it was able to get its hands on the knowledge required to design memory chips, it still needs the manufacturing expertise needed to produce them at scale. CXMT is the only new player that has successfully produced mainstream consumer DDR5 RAM, but it’s facing multiple allegations that it stole the technology needed to achieve that from Samsung. Even then, the DDR5 memory chips that the Chinese company produced don’t have the same performance as its competitors and track market prices, meaning it’s not the affordable alternative that many tech enthusiasts imagined it to be.

Sources indicate that the memory chip market is known for its boom-and-bust cycle, which is why manufacturers were initially reluctant to increase their capacity. But even if they started building factories at the first sign of a shortage, it would still take several years before these new facilities could start pumping out chips to ease the situation. Nevertheless, the three companies are presently facing a price-fixing lawsuit alleging that they coordinated their shift to HBM to cut DDR3 and DDR4 production, with the judge handling the case saying that it’s plausible they colluded as the market experienced the price surge.
